source_title: Effects of computerized prescriber order entry on pharmacy order-processing time
locator: Methods and Results; composition-to-pharmacist-verification and pharmacy-receipt-to-verification intervals
source_period: Before/after CPOE implementation; study period dates not reported in abstract (published 2009)
quantity: Mean time from prescriber composition to pharmacist verification
source_evidence_basis: An observational before/after study reports mean composition-to-verification time fell from 115 to 3 minutes after CPOE. The abstract also reports pharmacy-receipt-to-verification time fell from 31 to 3 minutes.
limitations: Single hospital and historical workflow comparison; implementation context and other changes may affect the comparison. Verification time does not measure dispensing, delivery, first administration, or current RWJ performance.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent order transmission and pharmacist verification as explicit timed stages, with an optional CPOE-era comparison scenario only when clearly labeled historical external evidence. Do not use the reported mean as an RWJ service-time distribution.
source_access: primary PubMed record and complete abstract inspected; article full text not available through accessed record

source_title: Effects of computerized prescriber order entry on pharmacy order-processing time
locator: Methods and Results; pharmacy receipt to pharmacist verification interval
source_period: Before/after CPOE implementation; study period dates not reported in abstract (published 2009)
source_n: 2,988 orders overall (1,488 pre, 1,500 post); sub-group counts not reported in abstract
source_evidence_basis: The reported interval begins when pharmacy receives an order and ends at pharmacist verification; it shortened from 31 minutes before CPOE to 3 minutes after CPOE in this hospital.
limitations: This measure ends at verification. It omits preparation/dispensing, transport to the nursing unit, administration readiness, medication availability, and bedside administration.
inferred_scenario_use: Keep verification completion separate from medication prepared, delivered, and administered states. Treat the source values as a historical external comparison, not a local baseline or service-time distribution.
source_access: primary PubMed record and complete abstract inspected; article full text not available through accessed record

source_title: Effect of Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission on 30-Day Returns to Hospital: A Randomized Clinical Trial
locator: Intervention; admission BPMH, pharmacist comparison, discrepancy communication and order adaptation
source_setting: Two regional secondary teaching hospitals in southern Switzerland; inpatient wards
value: Pharmacy assistant obtains a best possible medication history
Clinical pharmacist compares it with the physician-recorded home-medication list
Discrepancies are communicated to the attending physician and admission orders may be adapted
source_evidence_basis: The trial describes reconciliation as gathering a comprehensive current-medication history, comparing it with the admission list, then communicating discrepancies for clinician review and any needed order changes.
limitations: The intervention was studied in two Swiss hospitals and a selected high-risk population; staffing roles and procedures may differ elsewhere. This is a workflow reference, not RWJ policy.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent medication history capture, source comparison, discrepancy review, and clinician resolution as linked tasks with ownership and timestamps. Keep home medication history distinct from inpatient prescribing; do not encode drug or dose advice.
source_access: primary full text inspected via PMC/JAMA article

source_title: Effect of Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission on 30-Day Returns to Hospital: A Randomized Clinical Trial
locator: Results; discrepancies identified in intervention group during admission reconciliation
source_setting: Two regional secondary teaching hospitals in southern Switzerland; patients aged at least 85 years and/or with more than 10 admission medications
source_n: 866 intervention participants; 830 had at least one discrepancy
quantity: Intervention participants with at least one medication discrepancy
source_evidence_basis: Among 866 intervention participants, 830 (96.0%) had one or more discrepancies, with median 6 per patient (IQR 4–9). Omission was the most frequent discrepancy category reported.
limitations: Selected older and/or polypharmacy cohort; findings are not a general inpatient prevalence estimate. Detection is specific to the intervention and local medication-history process.
inferred_scenario_use: Use only as evidence that reconciliation may expose a substantial discrepancy workload in a selected cohort. If illustrating queues, label the cohort and keep counts distinct from local incidence; do not generate patient-specific medication content.
source_access: primary full text inspected via PMC/JAMA article

source_title: Effect of Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission on 30-Day Returns to Hospital: A Randomized Clinical Trial
locator: Primary outcome; unplanned all-cause hospital returns within 30 days after discharge
source_setting: Two regional secondary teaching hospitals in southern Switzerland; selected older/polypharmacy inpatient population
source_period: November 1, 2018 to January 15, 2020; outcome followed 30 days after discharge
quantity: Participants with composite unplanned hospital return within 30 days
source_evidence_basis: The randomized trial found 30-day unplanned visits or readmissions in 39.3% of intervention participants and 39.5% of controls (P=.93); the measured patient-centered endpoint did not differ.
limitations: This selected population and intervention do not establish that reconciliation is ineffective for other outcomes or settings. Do not interpret a null return outcome as evidence that discrepancies are harmless.
inferred_scenario_use: Separate process measures (history collected, discrepancies found/resolved) from downstream outcomes; do not assume a specific reduction in length of stay, readmission, or adverse events from completing a reconciliation task.
source_access: primary full text inspected via PMC/JAMA article

source_evidence_basis: AHRQ separates prescribing, communication/verification, dispensing, administration, and monitoring, while treating reconciliation and education as additional aspects; procurement and storage may also be included in the broader continuum.

locator: Chapter 1 medication-management continuum and evidence-report scope, printed pp. 2–3 (PDF pp. 30–31)

source_n: Not applicable; evidence synthesis and process framework
value: Order communication ends at transfer/clarification with pharmacy; dispensing and administration are later, distinct phases; monitoring follows administration.
source_evidence_basis: The report explicitly places dispensing after pharmacy communication and administration after dispensing, followed by monitoring; these are separately analyzed phases.
limitations: A conceptual boundary, not a quantitative estimate of delay or frequency. It does not define the target hospital’s electronic or manual event timestamps.
inferred_scenario_use: For an operations simulation, require separate event evidence for verified, prepared/dispensed, delivered, and administered states. Avoid inferring elapsed times between these states from the framework.

source_title: Observed rates of surgical instrument errors point to visualization tasks as being a critically vulnerable point in sterile processing and a significant cause of lost chargeable OR minutes
locator: Methods and Results; directly observed surgical instrument errors, case delays and delay duration
source_setting: Seven pediatric operating rooms at a two-hospital academic healthcare campus; elective OR days
source_period: Summer 2021; observation shifts during elective surgery days
source_n: 24 trained student observers; 236 errors in 147 cases; delay status documented for 103 of 147 error cases
quantity: Cases affected by delays and average delay time among cases with delay documentation
source_evidence_basis: Direct observers recorded 236 instrument errors across 147 cases. For the 103 cases with delay status documented, over half of inpatient and outpatient cases had delays; average time lost per case was 10.16 minutes.
limitations: Delay status was missing for 44/147 cases with errors; sampling occurred in pediatric ORs and may not represent adult or RWJ operations. The study estimates delays, not stockout probability or sterile-processing turnaround time.
inferred_scenario_use: Use as an external illustration that missing/broken/contaminated instruments can pause setup or operative progress. Do not apply its delay mean to RWJ or interpret it as instrument processing time.
source_access: primary full text inspected via PMC BioC; methods, results, and limitations reviewed

locator: Overview; sterilization cycle verification; physical facilities; cleaning, packaging, loading, and release
source_setting: CDC healthcare-facility infection prevention guidance for central processing and reusable patient-care instruments
source_period: Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities (2008), CDC page dated November 28, 2023; accessed 2026-10-10
source_n: Not applicable; official guidance, not a hospital throughput dataset
quantity: Instrument reprocessing stages and release dependencies
value: Receive and decontaminate used items
Inspect, assemble and package clean items
Load and run a cycle appropriate to the instruments and load
Monitor and release/quarantine according to cycle results
Store and distribute sterile items
source_evidence_basis: CDC describes sterile supply delivery as dependent on cleaning/decontamination, assembly and packaging, correct loading and cycle, monitoring, sterilant quality, and staff competence; failed verification requires quarantine rather than routine release.
limitations: Guidance describes process controls and infection-prevention practice, not device fleet size, consumable stock, cycle duration, daily capacity, or target-hospital policy details.
inferred_scenario_use: Treat used, in-process, sterile-released, stored, and case-carted instruments as distinct inventory states; include quarantined loads and reprocessing only when modeling the locally validated workflow. Do not infer local cycle duration or sterile inventory quantities.

locator: Sterilization Cycle Verification and Physical Facilities sections
source_period: Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities (2008), CDC page dated November 28, 2023; accessed 2026-10-10
source_n: Not applicable; official guidance, not a local equipment availability audit
quantity: Readiness dependencies for sterilizer and sterile storage
value: Sterilizer re-verification after installation, relocation, redesign, major repair, or failure
Indicator results gate routine release after verification
Separate decontamination, packaging, and sterilization/storage areas
Controlled sterile-storage access and conditions
source_evidence_basis: CDC says sterilizers require verification in specified change/failure situations and items remain quarantined until indicator results are acceptable; central processing areas separate decontamination, packaging, and sterilization/storage functions.
limitations: General guidance does not describe RWJ equipment count, maintenance state, consumable supplies, staffing, storage capacity, or exact local release criteria.
inferred_scenario_use: Model sterilizer out-of-service or a load on hold as separate from instrument-set stock, and only return resources after local verification/release. Confirm actual equipment, indicator supplies, and local process before assigning capacity or failure rates.

source_title: 2142. Understanding Errors in Sterile Processing of Surgical Instruments That Lead to Need for Immediate Use Sterilization in the Operating Room
locator: Abstract, Methods and Results; prospective 30-day SPD study of tray errors associated with immediate-use sterilization
source_setting: Hospital sterile processing department and operating rooms; institution type/size not stated in report
source_evidence_basis: In 30 days the department processed 17,348 trays for 1,868 procedures and identified 86 errors: 38 assembly, 30 sterilization, 10 case-cart, and 8 other. Ten assembly errors involved missing or incorrect instruments.
limitations: Short single-site study; error counts are not independently reported denominators by category, and identified errors were those associated with immediate-use sterilization. Do not treat as a general defect rate or RWJ estimate. This source is a published conference abstract, not a full-length study report.
inferred_scenario_use: Use as examples of assembly, sterilization-documentation, and case-cart failure states that can trigger rework or urgent instrument handling. Do not model routine throughput or local error probabilities from these counts.
source_access: primary published conference abstract inspected; no full-length study report inferred

source_title: 2142. Understanding Errors in Sterile Processing of Surgical Instruments That Lead to Need for Immediate Use Sterilization in the Operating Room
locator: Background, Methods and Conclusion; tray assembly, sterilization, and cart error categories; local immediate-use process description
source_setting: Single hospital SPD and operating rooms
quantity: Sterile instrument workflow error classes and response pressure
value: Tray assembly errors (including missing/incorrect instruments and filter placement)
Sterilization errors (including documentation errors)
Case-cart mistakes (including missing trays)
Immediate-use sterilization as a response to an instrument problem
source_evidence_basis: Investigators grouped observed events into assembly, sterilization, case-cart, and other errors; they identify process improvement opportunities in tray assembly to reduce immediate-use sterilization events.
limitations: The article describes one institution and its locally defined immediate-use cycle; it does not establish standard practice, routine cycle duration, or RWJ workflow. This source is a published conference abstract, not a full-length study report.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent unavailable or incorrect tray contents, sterilization documentation hold, and missing case-cart tray as distinct events that may prompt correction or escalation. Model emergency sterilization only if local policy validates the pathway.
source_access: primary published conference abstract inspected; no full-length study report inferred
